recentItems.title: Nepal-Tibet floods: Renewed sense of hope after people rescued from flooded tunnels
recentItems.description:
Three people have been found alive from different flooded tunnels in Nepal over the weekend following extensive search and rescue operations, 10 days after devastating floods swept through the country.

At least 1,344 people have been killed in Nepal in the floods that swept away houses, streets and schools in towns and villages near the border with China's Tibet, the disaster management authority said on Saturday.

An Australian team has arrived in Nepal to help search for those still missing — with 36 Australians among the more than 5,000 people unaccounted for as search crews continue to work through flood-hit communities.

As of Saturday, China said the death toll in Tibet was 31, with 531 others listed as missing, according to state media Xinhua.

Read more: https://www.sbs.com.au/news/article/three-rescued-from-flooded-tunnels-giving-families-renewed-hope-in-nepal/z7pqlb958

recentItems.title: Tony Mundine's family pays tribute to the late champion
recentItems.description:
The family of boxing great Tony Mundine OAM has spoken publicly for the first time since his death at a service held in inner-city Sydney, describing the proud Bundjalung man as a mentor "who offered a home away from home for many".

The Bundjalung boxing legend, who died on Sunday aged 75, was a champion who became the first Australian to fight in four different weight divisions.

He was remembered not only for his achievements in sport but also for his dedication to family and community.

recentItems.title: The hidden cost of living on one of the world’s oldest rainforests
recentItems.description:
The Daintree is recognised as one of the oldest rainforests in the world, attracting visitors from across the globe and a culturally significant place for the Kuku Yalanji people. 

But the UNESCO World Heritage site is also home to about 700 local residents, who live self-sufficiently off-grid, many reliant on diesel generators for electricity.

Growing uncertainty around fuel costs means powering their lives is becoming increasingly challenging, renewing calls for a renewable solution.

recentItems.title: El Niño driving extreme global heat causing 'disruption and devastation'
recentItems.description:
The United Nations has warned that El Niño is already disrupting lives around the world, with its "surging" climate pattern raising the risk of months of heatwaves, floods, drought and extreme weather.

The World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) said there is a "nearly 100 per cent" likelihood that El Niño will persist through to February, noting this is the first time an El Niño update has been so unequivocal.

The WMO's secretary-general, Celeste Saulo, said the climate driver, which was officially declared underway in June, has already dealt a blow to communities worldwide.

"We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods, and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies," she said.

The phenomenon is expected to peak at very high intensity towards the end of the year — potentially at a record-breaking level — with lasting effects on the climate well into 2027 and the prospect of unprecedented global heat.

recentItems.title: Voices heard in Nepal tunnel rescue effort
recentItems.description:
Australian rescue expert and engineer Arnold Dix says that voices have been heard from within a submerged tunnel during an ongoing rescue mission in flood decimated Nepal.

Dix, who has advised on multiple tunnel-collapse rescues, has been supporting the operation remotely and is travelling to Nepal to support teams on the ground.

Earlier on Friday, Dix, president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association, said teams at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project believed they had heard a faint response from inside the tunnel.

Rescue teams in Nepal have recovered more than 1,250 bodies, and more than 5,000 are missing, after the gigantic wave triggered by a rock and ice avalanche roared down the China-Nepal border.

recentItems.title: JD Vance says he 'wouldn't call it a war' with Iran
recentItems.description:
US Vice President JD Vance has said he would not categorise the Iran conflict as a ‘war’, despite continuing clashes with Iran six months after the start of hostilities.

"I wouldn't call it a war. Right now, there is no active shooting," Vance told a White House briefing when asked if the war would be over by US midterm elections in November.

Vance insisted that the US would not reopen talks with Iran until it ended attacks on commercial shipping.

The US administration has begun pushing the message that oil shipping is now stabilising as pressure from US voters continues to mount. on fuel prices.
